'''''Eucalyptus pulverulenta''''', commonly known as '''silver-leaved mountain gum''',<ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus pulverulanta'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20pulverulenta |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=7 December 2019}}</ref> is a species of straggly tree or [[Mallee (habit)|mallee]] that is [[Endemism|endemic]] to southern [[New South Wales]]. It has smooth bark, egg-shaped, heart-shaped or round, [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]] leaves arranged in opposite pairs, flower buds in groups of three, white flowers and cup-shaped to cylindrical fruit.

==Description==
''Eucalyptus pulverulenta'' is a straggly tree or mallee that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|5|m}} or a tree to {{cvt|9|m}}, and forms a [[lignotuber]]. It has smooth, greenish to grey or brown bark, sometimes hanging in short ribbons. The [[Crown (botany)|crown]] of the tree has almost exclusively juvenile leaves that are egg-shaped to round or heart-shaped, aromatic, [[wikt:Glaucous#Adjective|glaucous]], sessile, {{cvt|15-50|mm}} long, {{cvt|20-50|mm}} wide and arranged in opposite pairs. The flower buds are arranged in leaf [[wikt:axil|axil]]s in groups of three on an unbranched [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|3-12|mm}} long, the individual buds sessile or on [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] up to {{cvt|3|mm}} long. Mature buds are glaucous, oval to diamond-shaped, {{cvt|9-11|mm}} long, {{cvt|4-7|mm}} wide with a conical to beaked [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]. Flowering occurs from May to November and the flowers are white. The fruit is a woody, cup-shaped to cylindrical [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|5-10|mm}} long, {{cvt|6-11|mm}} wide with the valves near rim level.<ref name="ABRS" /><ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus pulverulenta'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_pulverulenta.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=30 May 2020}}</ref><ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=Ken |title=''Eucalyptus pulverulenta'' |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Eucalyptus~pulverulenta |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=7 December 2019}}</ref><ref name="environment">{{cite web |title=Approved Conservation Advice for ''Eucalyptus pulverulenta'' (Silver-leaved Mountain Gum) |url=http://www.environment.gov.au/biodiversity/threatened/species/pubs/21537-conservation-advice.pdf |publisher=Australian Government Department of te Environment |access-date=7 December 2019}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Eucalyptus pulverulenta'' was first formally described in 1819 by [[John Sims (taxonomist)|John Sims]] in the ''[[Curtis's Botanical Magazine|Botanical Magazine]]''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus pulverulenta''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/455890|publisher=APNI|access-date=7 December 2019}}</ref><ref name="Sims">{{cite journal |last1=Sims |first1=John |title=''Eucalyptus pulverulenta'' Heart-leaved Eucalyptus |journal=Curtis's Botanical Magazine |date=1819 |volume=46 |page=2087 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/14330#page/174/mode/1up |access-date=7 December 2019}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''pulverulenta'') is from the [[Latin]] word ''pulveratus'' meaning "powdered", referring to the white covering on the leaves, buds and fruit.<ref name="CANBR" />

==Distribution and habitat==
Silver-leaved mountain gum is only known from a few scattered populations on the [[Central Tablelands|Central]] and [[Southern Tablelands]] of New South Wales, between [[Bathurst, New South Wales|Bathurst]] and [[Bombala, New South Wales|Bombala]]. It grows in grassy woodland on hillsides and mountains.

==Conservation status==
This eucalypt is classified as "vulnerable" under the Australian Government ''[[Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999]]''. It was only known from about 5,400 plant in ten populations in 1990. The main threats to the species are habitat damage due to grazing, clearing of vegetation for fire trail, and its small population size.<ref name="environment" />

==Use in horticulture==
A cultivar known as 'Baby Blue' is a dwarf form of ''E. pulverulenta''.<ref name="aps">{{cite web |last1=Sheather |first1=Warren |last2=Sheather |first2=Gloria |title=''Eucalyptus pulverulenta'' |url=https://resources.austplants.com.au/plant/eucalyptus-pulverulenta/ |publisher=Australian Plants Society, N.S.W. |access-date=21 November 2021}}</ref>
